ecg-tachy-013.question: A patient with COPD presents with an acute respiratory exacerbation. Irregular narrow-QRS tachycardia at 120 bpm; each QRS is preceded by a P wave, but at least 3 different P-wave morphologies and variable PR intervals are identified. What is the diagnosis and what is the principle of treatment?
ecg-tachy-013.reponseAttendue: Multifocal atrial tachycardia. Treatment: correct the cause (respiratory decompensation, hypoxia, hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia, theophylline…); rate-slowing drugs (calcium channel blockers, possibly a cardioselective beta-blocker) if needed; electrical cardioversion is ineffective.
ecg-tachy-013.explication: Multifocal atrial tachycardia combines a rate > 100 bpm, at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and variable PP, PR and RR intervals. It is typically associated with decompensated chronic lung disease, hypoxia and metabolic disturbances. It is often mistaken for AF because of its irregularity, but the P waves are clearly distinct, with an isoelectric baseline. Treatment is first and foremost that of the underlying cause; electrical cardioversion and ablation have no first-line role.
ecg-tachy-013.aRetenir: Irregular tachycardia with ≥ 3 P-wave morphologies in a patient with respiratory failure = multifocal atrial tachycardia: treat the cause.

ecg-tachy-014.question: A 28-year-old woman reports palpitations of abrupt onset and offset. This tracing was recorded during an episode. What is the most likely diagnosis?
commentaires: Correct: regular narrow-QRS tachycardia, abrupt onset and offset, no visible P waves: AVNRT first and foremost.
Incorrect: the QRS complexes are narrow, without an RBBB-like pattern; the context suggests a junctional tachycardia.
Incorrect: the rhythm is perfectly regular.
Incorrect: abrupt onset and offset and no visible P waves before the QRS: this is not a sinus rhythm.
ecg-tachy-014.explication: On this tracing the tachycardia is regular with narrow QRS complexes at around 180 bpm and no visible P waves (retrograde P wave buried in the QRS). In a young woman with abrupt onset and offset, this picture first suggests AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT), the most common junctional tachycardia. AF is irregular. Sinus tachycardia, even when inappropriate, has a gradual onset and offset and visible P waves before each QRS. Fascicular VT has relatively narrow QRS complexes (often 120–140 ms) but with an RBBB-like pattern, which is not the case here. The main differential diagnosis remains orthodromic AVRT via an accessory pathway (concealed or manifest).
ecg-tachy-014.aRetenir: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia with abrupt onset/offset and no visible P waves: AVNRT first and foremost.

ecg-tachy-015.question: Which ECG sign, absent in sinus rhythm and visible during tachycardia, is most suggestive of typical (slow–fast) AVNRT?
options: A delta wave appearing during tachycardia
Retrograde P wave in the ST segment, > 90 ms after the QRS
Pseudo-r' in V1 and pseudo-S in the inferior leads
commentaires: Incorrect: a delta wave is a sign of pre-excitation in sinus rhythm, not of AVNRT.
Incorrect: a long RP of this kind rather points to orthodromic AVRT.
Incorrect: electrical alternans is mainly related to the fast rate and is not specific.
Correct: the retrograde P wave emerges at the end of the QRS, creating a pseudo-r' in V1 and a pseudo-S in the inferior leads.
ecg-tachy-015.explication: In typical AVNRT, atrial activation (retrograde, via the fast pathway) and ventricular activation are almost simultaneous: the retrograde P wave is therefore hidden in the QRS or emerges at its end. It produces a pseudo-r' in V1 and a pseudo-S in the inferior leads, to be compared with the sinus rhythm tracing. The RP interval is very short (typically < 70 ms). A retrograde P wave clearly separated from the QRS (RP > 70–90 ms) rather points to orthodromic AVRT. A delta wave is a sign of pre-excitation in sinus rhythm. Electrical alternans is more common in AVRT but is mainly related to the fast rate and is not specific.
ecg-tachy-015.aRetenir: Typical AVNRT: retrograde P wave "within" the end of the QRS = pseudo-r' in V1, pseudo-S in the inferior leads.

ecg-tachy-016.question: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at 200 bpm. A retrograde P wave (negative in the inferior leads) is seen in the ST segment, about 120 ms after QRS onset; RP < PR. What is the most likely mechanism?
commentaires: Incorrect: in typical AVNRT the RP is very short (< 70 ms), the P wave being buried in the QRS.
Incorrect: atypical AVNRT produces a long-RP tachycardia (RP > PR).
Correct: short RP but > 70 ms, retrograde P wave in the ST segment: retrograde conduction via the accessory pathway after the ventricles.
Incorrect: sinus tachycardia would show P waves positive in the inferior leads preceding the QRS.
ecg-tachy-016.explication: A short-RP tachycardia (RP < PR) with an RP > 70 ms is typical of orthodromic AVRT: the impulse travels down the AV node, activates the ventricles and then returns to the atria via the accessory pathway, which takes some time. In typical AVNRT the RP is much shorter (< 70 ms), the P wave being buried in the QRS. Atypical fast–slow AVNRT produces a long-RP tachycardia (RP > PR). Sinus tachycardia would show P waves positive in the inferior leads preceding the QRS. A definitive diagnosis remains electrophysiological.
ecg-tachy-016.aRetenir: Short RP but > 70 ms with a retrograde P wave in the ST segment: orthodromic AVRT.

ecg-tachy-017.question: Regular narrow-QRS long-RP tachycardia (RP > PR). Which diagnoses should be considered?
options: Orthodromic AVRT via a rapidly conducting accessory pathway
commentaires: Correct: the atrial P wave "conducts" to the next QRS, hence a long RP.
Correct: anterograde conduction via the fast pathway and slow retrograde conduction via the slow pathway: long RP.
Correct: posteroseptal accessory pathway with slow, decremental retrograde conduction; often incessant.
Incorrect: typical AVNRT is the very model of a very short-RP tachycardia.
Incorrect: a rapidly conducting accessory pathway produces a short-RP AVRT (> 70 ms), not a long RP.
ecg-tachy-017.explication: A long-RP tachycardia means that the P wave is closer to the next QRS than to the previous one. The three main diagnoses are atrial tachycardia (the P wave "conducts" to the next QRS), atypical fast–slow AVNRT (anterograde conduction via the fast pathway, slow retrograde conduction via the slow pathway) and permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia (PJRT, or Coumel tachycardia), which uses a posteroseptal accessory pathway with slow, decremental retrograde conduction. The latter, often incessant, can cause an arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy. Typical AVNRT, by contrast, is the very model of a very short-RP tachycardia, and orthodromic AVRT via a classic (rapidly conducting) accessory pathway produces a short RP, greater than 70 ms.
ecg-tachy-017.aRetenir: Long RP: atrial tachycardia, atypical AVNRT or PJRT (Coumel).

ecg-tachy-018.question: Termination of a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia with IV adenosine rules out atrial tachycardia.
commentaires: Incorrect: some focal atrial tachycardias (perinodal, triggered activity) are also terminated by adenosine.
Correct: it is the way the tachycardia terminates (on a P wave or on a QRS) that is informative, not termination itself.
ecg-tachy-018.explication: Adenosine terminates junctional tachycardias that use the AV node as part of their circuit (AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT), but some focal atrial tachycardias, particularly adenosine-sensitive ones (perinodal, triggered activity), are also terminated. Termination with adenosine therefore does not rule out atrial tachycardia. The way the tachycardia terminates is more informative: termination on a P wave (block in the AV node) argues against atrial tachycardia, since the atrial tachycardia would have to stop at the precise moment of AV block. When adenosine causes transient AV block with persisting atrial activity, an atrial tachycardia or flutter is unmasked. The ECG must always be recorded during the injection.
ecg-tachy-018.aRetenir: It is not termination with adenosine but the way the tachycardia terminates (or fails to) that guides the diagnosis.

ecg-tachy-019.question: During orthodromic AVRT, the development of functional left bundle branch block prolongs the VA interval and the tachycardia cycle length by about 40 ms. What can be concluded?
options: Right-sided accessory pathway, contralateral to the block
Left-sided accessory pathway, ipsilateral to the block
AVNRT: bundle branch block does not affect this circuit
commentaires: Incorrect: a block contralateral to the pathway does not alter the circuit; it is RBBB that slows AVRT via a right-sided pathway.
Correct: Coumel's law; the detour through the contralateral ventricle prolongs the VA, proving that a left-sided pathway is part of the circuit.
Incorrect: precisely, in AVNRT bundle branch block does not alter the cycle length; here it prolongs.
Incorrect: in atrial tachycardia, aberrancy does not alter the tachycardia cycle length.
ecg-tachy-019.explication: This is Coumel's law: when functional bundle branch block occurs on the same side as the accessory pathway, the activation wavefront must detour through the contralateral ventricle before reaching the pathway. The circuit lengthens, increasing the VA interval and the tachycardia cycle length (VA prolongation of around 35 ms or more for a lateral pathway). This phenomenon proves both the presence of an accessory pathway participating in the circuit and its laterality. In AVNRT or atrial tachycardia, bundle branch block does not alter the cycle length. Conversely, right bundle branch block that slows the tachycardia points to a right-sided pathway.
ecg-tachy-019.aRetenir: Cycle length prolongation with functional bundle branch block = accessory pathway ipsilateral to the block (Coumel's law).

ecg-tachy-020.question: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia. Which findings favour orthodromic AVRT over typical AVNRT?
options: Retrograde P wave visible in the ST segment with an RP > 70 ms
Slowing of the tachycardia when functional bundle branch block develops
Electrical alternans of the QRS, a specific sign of AVRT
Pseudo-r' wave in V1 during tachycardia, absent in sinus rhythm
commentaires: Correct: retrograde conduction via the accessory pathway after the ventricles separates the retrograde P wave from the QRS.
Correct: Coumel's law; block ipsilateral to the pathway lengthens the circuit and proves accessory pathway participation.
Incorrect: more common in AVRT, it depends mainly on rate and is not specific.
Incorrect: a pseudo-r' reflects a retrograde P wave fused with the QRS, typical of AVNRT.
ecg-tachy-020.explication: In orthodromic AVRT, retrograde atrial activation travels via the accessory pathway after ventricular activation: the retrograde P wave is separated from the QRS (RP > 70 ms) and often visible in the ST segment. Cycle length prolongation with functional bundle branch block ipsilateral to the pathway (Coumel's law) proves accessory pathway participation. Pre-excitation in sinus rhythm also makes AVRT very likely, although AVNRT may coexist. A pseudo-r' in V1, by contrast, reflects a retrograde P wave fused with the QRS and is typical of AVNRT. Electrical alternans, more common in AVRT, is mainly related to the fast rate: it is not specific.
ecg-tachy-020.aRetenir: RP > 70 ms, Coumel's law and pre-excitation in sinus rhythm favour AVRT.

ecg-tachy-021.question: Resting ECG of a 15-year-old boy being investigated for palpitations. What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
commentaires: Correct: short PR, slurred initial QRS upstroke (delta wave) and wide QRS: pre-excitation via an accessory pathway.
Incorrect: the PR is in fact short (< 120 ms).
Incorrect: bundle branch block widens the QRS without shortening the PR or creating a delta wave.
Incorrect: hyperkalaemia first causes peaked T waves and does not shorten the PR.
ecg-tachy-021.explication: On this tracing the PR is short, the QRS begins with a slurred upstroke (delta wave) and is widened. This triad of short PR (< 120 ms), delta wave and wide QRS reflects ventricular pre-excitation: part of the ventricle is activated early via an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node. The QRS is a fusion of activation via the accessory pathway and via the normal conduction system. Secondary repolarisation abnormalities are common and should not be mistaken for ischaemia. First-degree AV block prolongs the PR, bundle branch block does not shorten the PR, and hyperkalaemia first causes peaked T waves.
ecg-tachy-021.aRetenir: Short PR + delta wave + wide QRS = pre-excitation.

ecg-tachy-022.question: Wolff–Parkinson–White "syndrome" refers to ECG pre-excitation associated with symptomatic tachyarrhythmias; isolated asymptomatic pre-excitation is a WPW "pattern".
commentaires: Correct: pre-excitation + arrhythmia = syndrome; isolated pre-excitation = pattern, which is managed differently.
Incorrect: the statement is true; this distinction guides risk stratification in asymptomatic individuals.
ecg-tachy-022.explication: The terminology distinguishes the ECG pattern of pre-excitation (WPW pattern), often found incidentally, from WPW syndrome, which combines pre-excitation with arrhythmias (AVRT, pre-excited AF). This distinction has practical consequences: management of asymptomatic individuals relies on risk stratification (exercise test, Holter, or even an EP study), whereas symptomatic syndrome generally calls for ablation. The main risk, although rare, is sudden cardiac death from pre-excited AF degenerating into VF.
ecg-tachy-022.aRetenir: Pre-excitation + arrhythmia = WPW syndrome; pre-excitation alone = WPW pattern.

ecg-tachy-023.question: Pre-excitation with a delta wave negative in I and aVL, positive in II, III and aVF, and a dominant R wave from V1. Where is the accessory pathway probably located?
commentaires: Incorrect: a posteroseptal pathway produces a negative delta wave in III/aVF.
Incorrect: right-sided pathways produce an LBBB-like pattern with late transition, not a dominant R in V1.
Incorrect: an anteroseptal pathway produces a QS or rS pattern in V1.
Correct: the initial vector points away from I/aVL and anteriorly: negative delta in I/aVL, dominant R from V1.
ecg-tachy-023.explication: A left lateral pathway first activates the LV lateral wall, so the initial vector points away from I and aVL (negative delta wave) and anteriorly and rightward, producing a dominant R wave from V1. Right-sided pathways, by contrast, produce an LBBB-like pattern with a late transition (after V2–V3), because the right free wall is activated first. Anteroseptal pathways produce a delta wave positive in the inferior leads with QS/rS in V1, and posteroseptal pathways a delta wave negative in III/aVF. In practice, delta-wave polarity in V1 is the first step: positive (R > S) = left-sided pathway.
ecg-tachy-023.aRetenir: Negative delta in I/aVL and dominant R in V1: left lateral accessory pathway.

ecg-tachy-024.question: Pre-excitation with a clearly negative delta wave in II (and in III, aVF). According to the Arruda algorithm, which location should be suspected?
commentaires: Correct: negative delta in II = subepicardial posteroseptal pathway, accessible via the coronary sinus (middle cardiac vein).
Incorrect: anteroseptal pathways produce a positive delta wave in the inferior leads.
Incorrect: left lateral pathways produce a negative delta wave in I/aVL, not in II.
Incorrect: Mahaim fibres, which are decremental, generally do not produce manifest pre-excitation in sinus rhythm.
ecg-tachy-024.explication: In the Arruda algorithm, a negative delta wave in II is the marker of a subepicardial posteroseptal pathway, accessible from the coronary sinus or its middle cardiac vein, and sometimes associated with a coronary sinus diverticulum. This information is of major practical value: it prepares the operator for mapping within the coronary sinus (prior angiography is useful) rather than simple endocardial ablation. Anteroseptal pathways produce a positive delta wave in the inferior leads. Left lateral pathways produce a negative delta wave in I/aVL. Mahaim fibres, which are decremental, generally do not produce manifest pre-excitation in sinus rhythm.
ecg-tachy-024.aRetenir: Negative delta in II = epicardial posteroseptal pathway (coronary sinus).
